newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Clinton envoy in new crisis talks with Israel, PLO.
newsitem.headline: Clinton envoy in new crisis talks with Israel, PLO.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's Middle East peacemaker wades deeper into the mire of Israeli-PLO talks on Thursday in a new bid to seek an end to two months of crisis.

As envoy Dennis Ross prepared for separate sessions with Israaeli premier Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian president Yasser Arafat, officials from both sides were playing down hopes of an early breakthrough.

Ross, on his second shuttle mission in a month, met Netanyahu for 90 minutes of closed-door talks soon after arriving in Israel late on Wednesday. Officials declined comment on the substance of the talks.
After meeting Netanyahu and his defence and foreign ministers on Thursday, Ross is to meet Arafat in PLO-ruled Gaza.
Israeli and Palestinian officials cautioned against hopes of an early breakthrough.

"Ross will have difficult talks with the Palestinians, since Arafat will reject any resumption of talks -- which were halted by Israel when it decided to build Har Homa (a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem) -- until the bulldozers stop working," said one PLO official.
Israeli-PLO talks broke down in March after Netanyahu gave the final go-ahead to construction of thousands of homes for settlers at a hilltop site the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan said the work would go on.
"We obviously are not going to stop building in the settlements any more than the Palestinians are going to stop building in their towns," Bar-Illan said.
Israel has set a PLO crackdown on "terror" as its condition for resumed talks.

Ross's dogged shuttle diplomacy helped win the accord under which Israel withdrew from most of the West Bank town of Hebron in January. However his last mission in April was overshadowed by a domestic Israeli crisis and failed to win a breakthrough.
Bar-Illan said that while "there seems to be movement every time Dennis Ross is around" it would be wrong to expect dramatic developments from his mission.
The envoy's visit follows Israeli President Ezer Weizman's meeting with Arafat on Tuesday at the Israel-Gaza border.

Weizman, who has taken on a mediation role in his largely ceremonial position as president, said Arafat had agreed to resume security coordination between the sides. But the Tuesday talks failed to budge the sides from their demands for ending seven weeks of crisis.

Western officials and Palestinian sources said the Clinton administration would refrain at this stage from asking Netanyahu to freeze the settlement work, instead requesting "positive steps" such as granting Jerusalem Palestinians building permits, and pushing forward plans for a Palestinian port and airport.

Israel's ambassador to Washington said political pressure on the Jewish state -- coinciding with the Ross visit -- could be behind a press report that Israel tried to get a senior U.S. official to pass it a highly sensitive American document.

Ambassador Eliahu Ben Elissar, himself indirectly implicated in the Washington Post report published on Wednesday, strongly denied the story, saying it may have been an attempt to harm relations between Israel and its chief ally Washington.

Ties between the two countries were strained 12 years ago when a Jewish U.S. naval intelligence officer was caught passing data to Israel. The officer, Jonathan Pollard, pleaded guilty to spy charges in 1986 and is now serving a life sentence.

Relations have been further tested by Netanyahu's right-wing government, whose hardline policies have often run contrary to the policy guidelines of Washington, co-sponsor of the peace process with the Palestinians.
